item.title: Risk Factors for Osteoradionecrosis After Head and Neck Radiotherapy: A Systematic Review.
item.dc:creator: Le Guevelou J, Larnaudie A, Biau J, Chaux AG, Bourhis J, Pointreau Y
item.description:
Authors: Le Guevelou J, Larnaudie A, Biau J, Chaux AG, Bourhis J, Pointreau Y
Journal: Head & neck | DOI: 10.1002/hed.70546
Published: 2026-Nov-11
PMID: 43015994



Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Although intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) has led to a significant reduction in mandibular osteoradionecrosis (ORN) rates, head-and-neck radiotherapy (RT) is rapidly evolving-with increasing use of altered schedules and with novel systemic regimens including immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI). The aim of this work is to systematically review the established risk factors for ORN after head-and-neck RT and to provide a narrative outlook on emerging risk factors. MATERIAL AND METHODS: A systematic review of the literature was performed in September 2025 on three databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase and Scopus), using the MeSH terms "osteoradionecrosis" and "head and neck neoplasm." No language restriction was applied. Studies deemed eligible were studies reporting factors associated with the onset of osteoradionecrosis after photon-based head-and-neck RT. RESULTS: A total of 14 articles were included (1 prospective, 13 retrospective). The proportion of patients who developed ORN ranged from 1.8% to 19.8%, with a median interval from RT to ORN onset of 8 to 40 months. Pre-RT dental extraction (particularly within 7 days before RT start) and higher mandibular dose-volume parameters (V50Gy, V60Gy, dose to the primary site) were consistently associated with ORN onset. Smoking was associated with a shorter time to ORN onset, and bone surgery with resection of the periosteum was a strong independent risk factor (HR 5.87). No included study reported altered fractionation (accelerated, hyperfractionated) as being a risk factor to develop ORN. CONCLUSION: Risk factors for ORN include both patient-related (smoking) and treatment-related (pre-RT dental extraction, mandibular V50Gy/V60Gy) parameters. Whether these risk factors retain their relevance in modern altered-fractionation schedules and in ICI-combination regimens is currently unknown and warrants dedicated analysis from prospective studies.

item.title: Pharmacological chaperone treatment with Cystadane in aspartylglucosaminuria: an open-label, phase Ib/II trial.
item.dc:creator: Laine M, Banning A, Sairanen V, Lochnit G, Roine T, Harjunen EL, Roine U, Tokola AM, Terinkoski H, Leufkens D, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Laine M, Banning A, Sairanen V, Lochnit G, Roine T, Harjunen EL, Roine U, Tokola AM, Terinkoski H, Leufkens D, et al.
Journal: Nature communications | DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78752-x
Published: 2026-Nov-11
PMID: 43015321



Abstract:
This phase Ib/II investigator-initiated, open label trial aims to show the safety and efficacy of Cystadane (betaine) in aspartylglucosaminuria, a lysosomal storage disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, in Finnish patients homozygous for the Finnish major mutation, aged between 3 and 17 years at study begin (recruited: 25, analyzed: 21). Oral Cystadane efficacy and safety were studied over 48 months. The primary endpoint of the study, reduction of glycoasparagines in the urine, was quantitatively determined using liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry and normalized to urine creatinine. Urine glycoasparagines are significantly reduced upon Cystadane treatment (by 68.6% ±10.8%; p = 0.000), and the study thus meets its primary endpoint. Our data show that Cystadane/betaine efficiently improves the main disease biomarker, and it is safe to use in aspartylglucosaminuria. Further studies should be carried out in a larger patient population over a longer time to demonstrate the effects on disease progression. EudraCT registration number 2017-000645-48.

item.title: Prognostic significance of minor versus major extranodal extension in oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.dc:creator: Vaira LA, Qadeer H, Lechien JR, Maniaci A, Maglitto F, Salzano G, Iannella G, Chiesa-Estomba CM, Boscolo-Rizzo P, De Riu G
item.description:
Authors: Vaira LA, Qadeer H, Lechien JR, Maniaci A, Maglitto F, Salzano G, Iannella G, Chiesa-Estomba CM, Boscolo-Rizzo P, De Riu G
Journal: Oral oncology | DOI: 10.1016/j.oraloncology.2026.108220
Published: 2026-Nov-11
PMID: 43014091



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Extranodal extension (ENE) is an established adverse prognostic factor in oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC), but the clinical relevance of its extent remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the prognostic impact of quantitatively defined minor versus major ENE, with particular emphasis on the conventional 2-mm threshold. METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to August 2026. Studies of surgically treated OCSCC assessing pathological ENE extent and oncological outcomes were included. Random-effects meta-analyses using restricted maximum likelihood and Hartung-Knapp inference were performed when at least three compatible adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) were available. Risk of bias was assessed using QUIPS. RESULTS: Twenty-two reports representing 18 independent cohorts were included. Five studies contributed to the primary overall survival (OS) meta-analysis. Major ENE was associated with significantly worse OS than minor ENE (pooled HR 2.01, 95% CI 1.10-3.66; I2 = 60.5%). Three studies contributed to the disease-free survival (DFS) meta-analysis, showing a concordant but imprecise association (pooled HR 2.16, 95% CI 0.44-10.66; I2 = 59.3%). Alternative thresholds and morphological classifications also generally suggested poorer outcomes with increasing ENE extent. CONCLUSIONS: ENE extent provides prognostic information beyond binary ENE status in OCSCC. Major ENE is associated with worse OS, while evidence for DFS is directionally consistent but less precise. The 2-mm cutoff should be considered clinically useful but not yet biologically definitive.

item.title: Drought alters cowpea root endophytic fungal communities and functional characterization reveals plant growth-promoting potential of cultured endophytes.
item.dc:creator: Halo BA, Yaish MW
item.description:
Authors: Halo BA, Yaish MW
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0360553
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 43013566



Abstract:
Drought is a major constraint to cowpea productivity, but its effects on root-associated endophytic fungi remain poorly understood. This study investigated how drought influences cowpea root endophytic fungal communities and evaluated the plant growth-promoting potential of cultured fungal endophytes. Internal transcribed spacer (ITS) amplicon sequencing revealed that drought significantly altered fungal community composition. Several fungal taxa, including Aspergillus and Chaetomium, showed numerical differences in abundance under drought, although these taxon-specific differences were not significant after correction for multiple comparisons. In parallel, 13 fungal endophytes were isolated from drought-treated cowpea roots and evaluated for plant growth-promoting traits. The isolates differed in 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate (ACC) deaminase activity and presumptive indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) production, and several promoted wheat seedling growth under polyethylene glycol (PEG)-induced osmotic stress. Selected isolates also enhanced okra pollen germination under osmotic stress. Together, these findings demonstrate that drought alters the cowpea root endophytic fungal community and identify cultured endophytes with promising plant growth-promoting activities. Further evaluation through direct inoculation of cowpea under drought is needed to determine their potential for improving crop performance under water-limited conditions.

item.title: Computational evaluation of chromone-tetrazole hybrids as noncovalent inhibitors of SARS-CoV-2 Mpro.
item.dc:creator: Khibech O, Kadda S, Hammouti Y, Abadi S, Jodeh S, Hammouti B, Challioui A
item.description:
Authors: Khibech O, Kadda S, Hammouti Y, Abadi S, Jodeh S, Hammouti B, Challioui A
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0362385
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 43013528



Abstract:
Emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants continue to demand orally tractable, non-covalent inhibitors of the conserved main protease (Mpro). Here, chromone-phenyl-tetrazole hybrids were prioritized using a multiscale computational strategy that connects drug-likeness, binding stability, free-energy ranking, conformational behavior, and quantum-level electronic features. The series showed favorable oral drug-like profiles and low-to-moderate predicted acute toxicity. Among the stable Mpro complexes, M2 displayed the strongest computed affinity (MM/GBSA ΔGbind = -38.8 kcal·mol ⁻ ¹), driven mainly by dispersion with limited desolvation cost, whereas M4 showed the most direct catalytic-dyad engagement through His41/Cys145-supported anchoring. DFT analysis rationalized these complementary profiles: M2 and M4 exhibited narrower HOMO-LUMO gaps (4.00 eV) and higher electronic softness, while ELF/NCI maps revealed heteroatom-centered electron reservoirs and weak intramolecular preorganization. The derived pharmacophore consists of a planar chromone π-platform bearing a carbonyl/phenolic acceptor-donor edge, a para-phenyl spacer for conjugation and hydrophobic occupancy, and a methoxy-tetrazole polar/π-rich head for Glu166/Phe140/His163 anchoring. Overall, M2 and M4 emerge as complementary lead chemotypes for experimental validation and structure-guided optimization against Mpro.

item.title: Piloting cannabis for sleep disturbance in palliative care over 5 weeks: The pillow study protocol.
item.dc:creator: Newton AM, Krok-Schoen JL, Stevens EE, Babalonis SL, Wagener TL, Hinton A, Benzo R, Brasky TM
item.description:
Authors: Newton AM, Krok-Schoen JL, Stevens EE, Babalonis SL, Wagener TL, Hinton A, Benzo R, Brasky TM
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0361190
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 43013521



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep disturbance affects 60% of cancer patients, 3-fold that of the general population, and is frequently driven by clinical characteristics, physical symptoms, and psychological distress. Sleep disturbance and other symptoms often exacerbate one another, leading to reduced health-related quality of life (HRQOL). Sleep is the most commonly reported reason for cannabis use among adults with cancer, yet clinical evidence supporting its use for symptom management remains limited. OBJECTIVES: This report describes a protocol for a pilot randomized trial designed to evaluate the safety and feasibility of a cannabis-based intervention and to explore its preliminary efficacy for sleep disturbance and HRQOL. METHODS: This pilot parallel-arm randomized clinical trial will enroll 50 patients from the Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center (OSUCCC; anticipated Fall 2026). Eligible participants will be new to the OSUCCC's Palliative Care clinic and report at least moderate sleep disturbance. Participants will be randomized by sex and race strata to receive either usual care or a nightly oral cannabis gummy containing 5 mg Δ-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and 5 mg cannabidiol (CBD), taken 1 hour before bedtime for 30 days. Adverse events will be monitored throughout the study. Sleep, HRQOL, and related symptoms will be assessed using self-reported questionnaires, ecological momentary assessments, and actigraphy. CONCLUSIONS: Findings will provide critical safety, feasibility, and preliminary efficacy data to support a future large-scale, multisite trial targeting sleep disturbance and symptom palliation in cancer care.

item.title: Targeting DHFR to suppress one-carbon metabolism and enhance radiation sensitivity in patients with NRF2-active head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
item.dc:creator: Zolkind P, Wilkerson EM, Panda H, Chembo J, Sun J, Zhao K, Ley J, Atteberry M, Cho K, Wamsley NT, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Zolkind P, Wilkerson EM, Panda H, Chembo J, Sun J, Zhao K, Ley J, Atteberry M, Cho K, Wamsley NT, et al.
Journal: Clinical cancer research : an official journal of the American Association for Cancer Research | DOI: 10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-26-0700
Published: 2026-Nov-11
PMID: 43013352



Abstract:
PURPOSE: NRF2 hyperactivity is associated with radiation resistance in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). We evaluated the dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) inhibitors pyrimethamine and its potent analog, WCDD115, as radiosensitizing agents through disruption of one-carbon metabolism. PATIENTS AND METHODS: Preclinical studies used NRF2-competent and deficient HNSCC models, clonogenic assays, transcriptomics, metabolomics, pharmacokinetics/toxicity testing, and syngeneic tumor grafts to assess WCDD115 as a novel radiosensitizing agent. In parallel, we conducted an open-label, single-center, window-of-opportunity early phase I clinical trial (NCT05678348) of previously untreated patients with HPV(-) stage III/IV HNSCC to receive pyrimethamine 50mg prior to surgery. Correlative analysis included mass spectrometry, western blotting, and pathway analysis. RESULTS: WCDD115 enhanced radiation-induced DNA damage and suppressed one-carbon metabolism and nucleotide biosynthesis. Parallel mouse tumor studies demonstrated that WCDD115 enhanced the efficacy of radiation in NRF2-competent but not NRF2-deficient tumors. In a clinical trial of neoadjuvant pyrimethamine, DHFR protein expression was enriched post-treatment by a mean fold change of 9.91 (95% confidence interval 8.1 to 12.2), consistent with a strong on-target effect. The drug was well tolerated with no drug-related grade 3-5 adverse events or surgical delays. CONCLUSIONS: NRF2 hyperactivity is associated with enhanced one-carbon metabolism which can be therapeutically targeted with DHFR inhibitors to promote radiation sensitization. In HNSCC patients, pyrimethamine achieves potent DHFR inhibition and a favorable safety profile supporting a future phase 2 trial integrating pyrimethamine with definitive radiation-based therapy for NRF2-active HNSCCs.

item.title: HOPO 14-1, an Oral Actinide Chelator: A Phase 1 Nonrandomized Clinical Trial.
item.dc:creator: Goonewardena SN, Atleski L, Bunin DI, Furimsky AM, Pui S, Green CE, Chang PY
item.description:
Authors: Goonewardena SN, Atleski L, Bunin DI, Furimsky AM, Pui S, Green CE, Chang PY
Journal: JAMA | DOI: 10.1001/jama.2026.19809
Published: 2026-Nov-11
PMID: 43013314



Abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Current treatments approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for internal actinide contamination (pentetate calcium trisodium and pentetate zinc trisodium) require intravenous injection or nebulized inhalation under medical supervision and have limited radionuclide coverage. HOPO 14-1, an oral form of 3,4,3-LI(1,2-HOPO), is the first shelf-stable, broad-spectrum actinide chelator in clinical development that does not require intravenous access or trained personnel. In preclinical models, 3,4,3-LI(1,2-HOPO) removed a broad range of actinides, and its oral route supports scalable emergency medical use. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetic parameters, and excretion of a single dose of HOPO 14-1 in healthy adults. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This was a phase 1 nonrandomized clinical trial including 42 healthy adults (6 per dose level) with evaluations for 14 days after administration of a single dose and conducted at a single site in the US. Participants were recruited and screened between March 2023 and July 2025 and follow-up was completed in August 2025. INTERVENTION: Single oral dose of HOPO 14-1 administered at 1 of 7 dose levels (100 mg, 200 mg, 500 mg, 1200 mg, 2500 mg, 5000 mg, or 7500 mg) with follow-up through day 14 after dose administration. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcomes were the incidence and severity of adverse events, drug-related adverse events, and serious adverse events. The secondary outcomes were plasma pharmacokinetic parameters and cumulative urinary and fecal excretion. RESULTS: Of the 42 healthy adults enrolled (median age, 43 [IQR, 34-51] years; 64% female), all received a single dose of HOPO 14-1 (administered across all dose levels as assigned). There were no serious adverse events or dose-limiting toxic effects. The drug-related adverse events included diarrhea (31%), vomiting (14%), headache (12%), and fatigue (7%); all were mild to moderate in severity. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the principal tolerability findings and most evident at the highest doses. The plasma pharmacokinetic parameters demonstrated rapid absorption (median time of maximum plasma concentration, 0.86 [range, 0.53-1.60] hours to 1.90 [range, 1.40-2.90] hours) and dose-dependent increases in systemic exposure, with greater than proportional increases at higher doses. Fecal excretion was the primary route of elimination; urinary excretion was minimal. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Single oral doses of HOPO 14-1 up to 7500 mg were administered without dose-limiting toxicity or serious adverse events in healthy adults. Gastrointestinal tolerability defined the practical single-dose ceiling. These findings establish the first human safety and pharmacokinetic profile of a novel, orally administered actinide chelator and support further clinical evaluation of HOPO 14-1 as a countermeasure for internal radionuclide and heavy metal contamination. Development of a deployable and population-level emergency intervention addresses a long-standing unmet need with important implications for public health preparedness. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05628961.

item.title: Body composition and risks of head and neck cancers: evidence from a large-scale population-based cohort.
item.dc:creator: Li J, Li B, Qiu K, Deng D, Cheng D, Pang W, Song Y, Rao Y, Zhao Y, Ren J
item.description:
Authors: Li J, Li B, Qiu K, Deng D, Cheng D, Pang W, Song Y, Rao Y, Zhao Y, Ren J
Journal: Cancer causes & control : CCC | DOI: 10.1007/s10552-026-02281-7
Published: 2026-Nov-11
PMID: 43012887



Abstract:
PURPOSE: This study aimed to investigate the association between body compositions with overall/subtype-specific HNC risks. METHODS: We included participants from the UK Biobank with complete body composition data and without other cancers. Prospective analysis further excluded prevalent HNC. Multivariable logistic and Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to assess the associations. Subgroup analysis was stratified by age, sex, and smoking status. RESULTS: Among 399,640 participants included, 1,342 HNC cases were identified. Multiple body composition measures showed protective effects against overall HNC, including body mass index (BMI, overweight: odds ratio [OR] = 0.76, p < 0.001; obese: OR = 0.67, p < 0.001) and fat percentage of the whole-body (OR = 0.78, p < 0.001), trunk (OR = 0.81, p < 0.001), legs (OR = 0.74, p < 0.001), and arms (OR = 0.80, p < 0.001). Fat-free mass (FFM) of the whole-body (OR = 0.98, p < 0.001), trunk (OR = 0.95, p < 0.001), legs (OR = 0.88, p < 0.001) and arms (OR = 0.70, p < 0.001) also demonstrated protective effects. The majority of these associations were significant in young males and ever-smokers, and the effects of FFM remained significant in old males and females. Additionally, site-specific body composition factors showed complex relationships with HNC subtypes and the prospective analysis confirmed most observed associations. CONCLUSION: BMI, fat percentage, and FFM were associated with lower risk of overall HNC, functioning mainly in males and old females.

item.title: Treatment Hotspots and Controversies in Papillary Thyroid Microcarcinoma.
item.dc:creator: Yu L, Liu F, Wang F, Yuan S, Zhao X, Gu S, Guo R, Zhao J, Zhang W
item.description:
Authors: Yu L, Liu F, Wang F, Yuan S, Zhao X, Gu S, Guo R, Zhao J, Zhang W
Journal: The oncologist | DOI: 10.1093/oncolo/oyag216
Published: 2026-Nov-10
PMID: 43010779



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The significant global rise in the detection rate of papillary thyroid microcarcinoma (PTMC) has sparked intense debates concerning overdiagnosis and overtreatment. Consequently, therapeutic strategies are shifting from radical surgery toward risk-stratified management, including active surveillance (AS) and minimally invasive techniques (MIT). Core controversies focus on the necessity of surgical intervention, the extent of prophylactic central neck dissection, and selection criteria for MIT versus conventional surgery. METHODS: This review systematically evaluates the comparative evidence on AS, thermal ablation (TA), and surgical treatment for PTMC, highlighting divergent Eastern and Western management philosophies to provide an optimized framework for clinical decision-making. RESULTS: Although AS demonstrates favorable survival benefits and health economic advantages for patients with PTMC, unresolved clinical risks persist. Notably, Chinese guidelines adopt stricter standards compared to the international 10 mm threshold. Among MIT, TA exhibits well-established short-term efficacy; however, recent expert consensus emphasizes a strict therapeutic hierarchy to prevent misuse, given the paucity of long-term recurrence data. CONCLUSION: An individualized framework based on risk stratification is essential for PTMC management, balancing oncological safety and quality of life.

item.title: Current Evidence of Precision Medicine via Multi-Omic Approaches in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma.
item.dc:creator: Leoni ER, Abbenante ED, Contrera KJ, Unrue KC, Hanania AN, Kansara SG
item.description:
Authors: Leoni ER, Abbenante ED, Contrera KJ, Unrue KC, Hanania AN, Kansara SG
Journal: Head & neck | DOI: 10.1002/hed.70544
Published: 2026-Nov-10
PMID: 43010591



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Perioperative and adjuvant immunotherapy are new standards of care for selected patients with resectable locoregionally advanced HPV-negative HNSCC, but low pathologic response rates and a lack of predictive biomarkers limit patient selection and response-adapted care. This review examines multi-omic approaches to predicting immunotherapy response and personalizing therapy. METHODS: A narrative review of current multi-omic strategies for HNSCC was performed. Data providing predictive, prognostic, diagnostic, surveillance, or exploratory value was summarized. RESULTS: Multi-omics may identify those likely to benefit from immunotherapy. Single-cell transcriptomics reveals changes in the tumor immune microenvironment while spatial proteomics reveals tertiary lymphoid structures, dendritic cell networks, and protein signatures predicting immunotherapy response. Obstacles include unstandardized protocols, limited prospective validation, and small sample sizes. CONCLUSIONS: Multi-omics can reshape biomarker-driven HNSCC care, but implementation requires prospective validation, standardized protocols, and multi-platform integration.

item.title: Prognostic value of lymph node ratio beyond extranodal extension in node-positive oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma.
item.dc:creator: Kumar A, Laskar SG, Sharma P, Sinha S, Mohanty S, Budrukkar A, Swain M, Pantvaidya G, Nair D, Thiagarajan S, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Kumar A, Laskar SG, Sharma P, Sinha S, Mohanty S, Budrukkar A, Swain M, Pantvaidya G, Nair D, Thiagarajan S, et al.
Journal: Radiotherapy and oncology : journal of the European Society for Therapeutic Radiology and Oncology | DOI: 10.1016/j.radonc.2026.111863
Published: 2026-Nov-10
PMID: 43008829



Abstract:
PURPOSE: Extranodal extension (ENE) is a key determinant of adjuvant therapy in node-positive oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC). However, conventional nodal staging may not fully capture the quantitative burden of nodal disease. We evaluated whether lymph node ratio (LNR) provides additional prognostic value beyond ENE in a large randomized trial cohort. METHODS AND MATERIALS: We performed a retrospective subgroup analysis of 661 node-positive patients from the phase III randomized Oral Cavity Adjuvant Therapy (OCAT) trial. LNR was defined as the metastatic-to-dissected lymph node ratio and categorized as low (<0.10) or high (≥0.10). Overall survival (OS), recurrence-free survival (RFS), and locoregional control (LRC) were estimated using Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression, adjusting for ENE, T stage, N stage, PNI, margin status, LVI, and treatment arm. RESULTS: With a median follow-up of 91 months, 387 deaths occurred. On multivariable analysis, high LNR remained independently associated with inferior OS (HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.15-1.78; p = 0.001), RFS (HR 1.48; p = 0.001), and LRC (HR 1.40; p = 0.018). High LNR/ENE-positive patients had significantly worse survival than the reference group, low LNR/ENE-negative (HR 2.08, 95% CI 1.47-2.95; p < 0.001). Low LNR/ENE-positive patients trended toward inferior survival (HR 1.36; p = 0.051), while high LNR/ENE-negative patients showed no significant difference (HR 1.12; p = 0.65). CONCLUSIONS: LNR is an independent prognostic factor beyond ENE across OS, RFS, and LRC in node-positive OCSCC. High LNR combined with ENE identifies a distinctly high-risk subgroup, whereas high LNR alone did not significantly impact survival in the absence of ENE. Incorporating LNR into postoperative risk stratification may refine identification of patients for risk-adapted adjuvant strategies.

item.title: A tumor biology-informed interpretation of TNM 9 in HPV-associated OPSCC.
item.dc:creator: Hoffmann M, Tribius S
item.description:
Authors: Hoffmann M, Tribius S
Journal: Oral oncology | DOI: 10.1016/j.oraloncology.2026.108227
Published: 2026-Nov-10
PMID: 43008667



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The 9th edition of the TNM classification (TNM-9) refines anatomical staging in head and neck cancer, maintaining p16-based categorization for HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC). However, anatomical extent alone does not capture key biological and host-related determinants of clinical behavior. METHODS: In this concept-driven synthesis, we integrate TNM-9 anatomy with evidence on transcriptional viral activity, p16 discordance, nodal morphology including imaging-defined extranodal extension (iENE), immune microenvironment, and host modifiers such as smoking and comorbidity. We propose a layered integrative framework that preserves TNM-9 structure while contextualizing tumor biology. The review is based on a selective synthesis of key translational and clinical studies identified through literature searches and expert knowledge, without a formal systematic approach. RESULTS: TNM-9 improves anatomical prognostic stratification at the population level, but identical anatomical stages encompass biologically heterogeneous entities. HPV RNA expression distinguishes biologically favorable tumors from p16+/HPV-inactive disease. iENE retains prognostic relevance in HPV-associated OPSCC, although its radiological appearance may partly reflect immune-associated stromal remodeling and cystic nodal morphology rather than invasive behavior alone. Smoking exposure, comorbidity burden, and immune-related host factors modify survival independent of tumor extent, explaining different outcomes within identical TNM stages. CONCLUSIONS: TNM-9 should be interpreted as an anatomical framework supplemented by biological and host factors. A multidimensional understanding enhances clinical applicability, avoids overtreatment of biologically favorable disease and highlights high-risk phenotypes concealed by anatomy alone. This perspective supports precise, biology-informed risk assessment in HPV-associated OPSCC. .

item.title: Treatment of Recurrent and/or Metastatic Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma: CSCO and ASCO Joint Guideline.
item.dc:creator: Jiang W, Ismaila N, Chua ML, Haddad R, Le QT, Colevas AD, Saba NF, Harrington K, Huang SH, Chan AT, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Jiang W, Ismaila N, Chua ML, Haddad R, Le QT, Colevas AD, Saba NF, Harrington K, Huang SH, Chan AT, et al.
Journal: Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology | DOI: 10.1200/JCO-26-02650
Published: 2026-Nov-10
PMID: 43008245



Abstract:
PURPOSE: To provide evidence-based recommendations on first- and subsequent-line systemic therapy, maintenance therapy, locoregional consolidation, and salvage local therapy for patients with recurrent and/or metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). METHODS: A multidisciplinary Expert Panel convened by CSCO and ASCO reviewed evidence from randomized trials, meta-analyses, systematic reviews, prospective and retrospective studies, and clinical experience. The guideline was informed by a systematic literature review and consensus-based interpretation of efficacy, safety, feasibility, and patient-centered outcomes across scenarios. Outcomes included overall and progression-free survival, response and disease control rates, toxicity, and quality of life. RESULTS: Evidence supports platinum-based chemotherapy plus a programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) inhibitor as preferred first-line therapy for medically fit patients. Evidence also supports maintenance strategies after disease control, while treatment selection depends on prior treatment, disease extent, patient fitness, resource availability, and preferences. Selected responders may receive locoregional consolidation radiotherapy or oral maintenance chemotherapy. For isolated locoregional recurrence amenable to local therapy, options include salvage surgery and re-irradiation. RECOMMENDATIONS: Chemotherapy plus a PD-1 inhibitor, followed by maintenance PD-1 inhibition for up to 2 years, should be offered first-line to appropriate patients with recurrent and/or metastatic NPC. Chemotherapy alone may be offered when immunotherapy is unsuitable or declined. Selected patients responding to first-line chemotherapy may receive oral maintenance chemotherapy or locoregional consolidation intensity-modulated radiotherapy. Salvage surgery or re-irradiation is recommended for appropriately selected patients with isolated locoregional recurrence. Subsequent-line options include chemotherapy, PD-1 inhibitors, and antibody-drug conjugates. Treatment should be individualized according to disease setting, prior therapy, expected toxicities, availability, local drug approvals, and patient preferences. Early supportive and specialist interdisciplinary palliative care, where available, should accompany active anticancer treatment for advanced, incurable disease.Additional information is available at www.ascopubs.org/topics/asco-guidelines/head-neck-cancer.

item.title: Treatment of Stage IB to III Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma: CSCO-ASCO Guideline Update.
item.dc:creator: Chen YP, Ismaila N, Huang SH, Jiang W, Ma B, Haddad R, Le QT, Colevas AD, Harrington K, Yom SS, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Chen YP, Ismaila N, Huang SH, Jiang W, Ma B, Haddad R, Le QT, Colevas AD, Harrington K, Yom SS, et al.
Journal: Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology | DOI: 10.1200/JCO-26-02648
Published: 2026-Nov-10
PMID: 43008242



Abstract:
PURPOSE: To update the 2021 CSCO-ASCO guideline on chemotherapy in combination with radiotherapy for the definitive treatment of non-metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), incorporating new evidence on radiotherapy techniques and target-volume de-escalation, chemotherapy regimens and their sequencing, adjuvant therapy, and immunotherapy for patients with stage IB-III disease. METHODS: A multidisciplinary Expert Panel reviewed evidence published since the prior guideline, including randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and relevant prospective and retrospective studies. Outcomes of interest included overall survival, failure-free or progression-free survival, locoregional and distant disease control, acute and late toxicities, and patient-reported quality of life. Recommendations were developed using the ASCO guideline development process and Expert Panel consensus. RESULTS: The updated evidence supports: IMRT with image guidance and MRI-based target delineation as core components of definitive treatment; selected response-adapted target delineation following induction chemotherapy; elective nodal de-escalation in appropriately selected patients; risk-adapted chemotherapy sequencing according to stage and biologic risk; cisplatin-based concurrent chemoradiotherapy; gemcitabine-cisplatin (GP) or docetaxel-cisplatin-fluorouracil (TPF) as preferred induction regimens; and selected adjuvant chemotherapy options, including metronomic capecitabine for patients with higher residual post-chemoradiotherapy risk. Several randomized trials evaluating PD-1 inhibitors have demonstrated improved disease-control outcomes, but overall survival data remain immature. RECOMMENDATIONS: This guideline update provides recommendations on radiotherapy technique, dose, imaging, and target delineation; sequencing of additional chemotherapy with radiotherapy; concurrent chemotherapy options; induction chemotherapy regimens and timing; adjuvant chemotherapy options; and the role of immunotherapy. At present, the Panel makes no recommendation for or against routine addition of immunotherapy to induction-concurrent chemoradiotherapy; applicability of the trial evidence, benefits and harms, local approval and access, and patient preferences should guide individualized decisions.Additional information is available at www.ascopubs.org/topics/asco-guidelines/head-neck-cancer.

Abstract:
Weaning stress caused by maternal separation and dietary changes often leads to intestinal disorders such as diarrhea and enteritis in young animals, and the development of antibiotic-free, safe preparations to manage these conditions is therefore a promising strategy. The optimal proportion of each component in the formulation was determined in our preliminary study using orthogonal experimental design and range analysis. This study first evaluated the effects of glycyrrhizic acid and Isatidis folium extract on the growth of Bacillus subtilis (B. subtilis), and then examined the effects of the compound preparation (CP) composed of glycyrrhizic acid, Isatidis folium extract, and B. subtilis on in vitro antibacterial activity, growth performance, immune modulation, and the amelioration of dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis in Hu sheep. item.title: Prevalence of human papillomavirus and HPV vaccination among cisgender bisexual women: Protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.dc:creator: Lawley KA, Kusuma K, Farquhar SA, Goodreau SM, Winer RL
item.description:
Authors: Lawley KA, Kusuma K, Farquhar SA, Goodreau SM, Winer RL
Journal: PloS one | DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0360427
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 43008003



Abstract:
Human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted infection in the United States, and a primary cause of cervical cancer. Although cervical cancer is largely preventable through HPV vaccination, vaccine coverage remains suboptimal. Research on HPV prevalence and vaccination among cisgender bisexual women is limited and inconsistent. This may be partly due to variation in how bisexuality is defined. Bisexuality may be operationalized based on sexual identity (e.g., self-identification as bisexual) or sexual behavior (e.g., sexual contact with more than one sex or gender), and these differing definitions may capture distinct populations and yield divergent health findings. This paper proposes a protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis to examine whether reported HPV prevalence and vaccination rates among cisgender bisexual women differ based on whether bisexuality is defined by identity or behavior. The protocol is registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251252015) and follows PRISMA-P guidelines. Random-effects meta-analyses will estimate pooled HPV prevalence and vaccination rates by definition type. Findings will clarify how operational definitions shape observed HPV-related outcomes and inform tailored cervical cancer prevention strategies for cisgender bisexual women.

item.title: Lymphopenia and Circulating Biomarker Dynamics Associated with Clinical Outcome and Toxicity in Pazopanib-Treated Radioiodine-Refractory Thyroid Cancer: Exploratory Analyses from the Pazothyr Trial.

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pazopanib showed clinical activity in progressive radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid carcinoma (RAIR-DTC), although its use is limited by substantial toxicity not reduced by intermittent treatment. We aimed to identify biomarkers associated with outcome and treatment-related toxicity in these patients. METHODS: This study reported exploratory results related to the Pazothyr trial (NCT01813136) investigating pazopanib efficacy in RAIR-DTC patients. We evaluated lymphopenia and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) from the Pazothyr clinical database (n = 168). Dedicated informed consent for additional plasma and tumor sample collection allowed quantification of plasma angiogenic factors and cytokines at baseline and after one month of pazopanib (n = 111). Immune markers (CD8, FOXP3, CD163, and PDL1) analyzed by immunohistochemistry in archived primary tumors from patients (n = 68) with response or stable disease after 6 months of pazopanib were scored semiquantitatively. Associations with response, progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and substantial treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were evaluated. Given the exploratory nature of this study, no adjustment for multiple comparisons was performed. RESULTS: At baseline, moderate and severe lymphopenia were associated with shorter PFS, unlike high NLR. Elevated Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor A (VEGF-A), Interleukin 6 (IL-6), and CXCL8 correlated with poorer PFS. High VEGF-A, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), IL-6, CXCL8, and CXCL9 were associated with shorter OS. X Early changes in placental growth factor (PlGF), HGF, interleukin 12 subunit p40, and CXCL10 were associated with substantial TRAEs. Multivariable analyses identified baseline severe lymphopenia (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.39 [confidence interval or CI 1.27-4.48], p = 0.007) and high CXCL8 (HR = 2.01 [CI 1.26-3.21], p = 0.004) as independent factors associated with progression. High baseline NLR (HR = 2.26 [CI 1.21-4.22], p = 0.01), HGF (HR = 2.37 [CI 1.33-4.20], p = 0.003), and CXCL8 (HR = 2.20 [CI 1.25-3.87], p = 0.006) were similarly associated with death. One-month increases in PlGF (odds ratio [OR] = 2.49 [CI 1.13-5.50], p = 0.024) and HGF (OR = 2.91 [CI 1.32-6.43], p = 0.008) were independently associated with substantial TRAEs. In patients with tumor samples, Programmed cell Death-Ligand 1 (PDL1)-immune cell score (ICS) >1% (HR = 2.05 [CI 1.15-3.66], p = 0.015) was also associated with progression. CONCLUSIONS: Baseline lymphopenia and inflammatory plasma biomarkers were associated with clinical outcome, whereas early changes in circulating factors were associated with substantial TRAEs. These exploratory results require prospective validation in RAIR-DTC patients treated with pazopanib or other VEGF receptor-targeting multikinase inhibitors. The relevance of PDL1-ICS expression for anti-PD1/PDL1-based therapies requires dedicated prospective trials.

Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: High-fidelity simulation may improve surgical training in head and neck surgery, yet validated perfused cadaveric models remain scarce. We evaluated the face, content, and construct validity of a perfused cadaveric model using isolated cephalic perfusion for cervicofacial surgical simulation. STUDY DESIGN: Prospective validation study of a reperfused cadaveric model using SIMLIFE® technology. SETTING: Institute of Anatomy and Surgical Simulation, Toulouse University Hospital. METHODS: Twenty unilateral levels I to IV neck dissections were performed on 11 body donors using a perfused SIMLIFE® model with isolated cephalic perfusion. Seven experts and 5 residents participated. Face and content validity were assessed using Likert-scale questionnaires, whereas construct validity was evaluated using the Onco-Neck-Score through blinded video assessment. RESULTS: High face validity was demonstrated across most assessed domains, particularly venous wall consistency, venous coloration, nerve appearance, and bleeding flow following vascular injury. Experts rated the model as highly relevant for resident training and surgical skills acquisition. Construct validity was supported by significantly higher Onco-Neck-Score values among experts compared with residents (70.8 [interquartile range 68.8-71.0] vs 58.2 [interquartile range 53.8-61.9], P < .001). It provides a realistic environment for neck dissection simulation and may represent a promising tool for surgical education and competency assessment.

item.title: Bioactive Peptide HX-12C Ameliorates Oral Submucous Fibrosis via Inhibition of TGF-β/Smad-Driven Myofibroblast Activation: A Potential Therapeutic Strategy.

item.description:
Authors: Huang W, Shi R, Wang Y, Wang X, Qin Z, Luo X, Li K, Wang B, Hu Y
Journal: Oral diseases | DOI: 10.1111/odi.70569
Published: 2026-Nov-10

Abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To investigate the anti-fibrotic effects and mechanism of action of the bioactive peptide HX-12C in oral submucous fibrosis. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Primary human buccal mucosal fibroblasts were treated with arecoline to induce a myofibroblast phenotype. The effects of HX-12C on cell proliferation, migration and fibrotic markers were assessed. Molecular docking and immunofluorescence were used to examine HX-12C binding to transforming growth factor-beta receptor I, validated by the inhibitor SB-431542. In vivo efficacy was evaluated in a bleomycin-induced rat model of oral submucous fibrosis. RESULTS: HX-12C promoted fibroblast proliferation and migration but suppressed arecoline-induced myofibroblast activation, downregulating alpha-smooth muscle actin, fibronectin and collagens I/III. Mechanistically, HX-12C bound to transforming growth factor-beta receptor I, inhibited SMAD2/3 phosphorylation and downstream pro-fibrotic gene expression, effects attenuated by SB-431542. In vivo, HX-12C improved mouth opening and reduced collagen deposition. CONCLUSIONS: HX-12C exerts potent anti-fibrotic effects by directly targeting transforming growth factor-beta receptor I and inhibiting the canonical transforming growth factor-beta/Smad signalling pathway. Our findings identify HX-12C as a promising therapeutic candidate for oral submucous fibrosis and provide a rationale for developing peptide-based therapies for transforming growth factor-beta-driven fibrotic diseases.

item.title: Betel-Quid Exposure and Site-Specific Prognostic Patterns in Oral Cavity Squamous Cell Carcinoma.

Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Betel-quid chewing is a risk factor for oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC), but its associations with tumour subsite and depth-of-invasion (DOI) related prognosis remain unclear. We examined site-specific associations and exposure-stratified DOI thresholds for disease-specific survival (DSS). METHODS: This retrospective cohort included 454 patients from southern Thailand. Tumour-subsite associations were assessed using multivariable logistic regression. Exploratory DSS thresholds were derived among surgically treated patients using maximally selected log-rank statistics and evaluated with an exposure-stratified Cox model. RESULTS: Of 454 patients, 154 (33.9%) were betel chewers. Exposure was associated with tumours of the buccal mucosa (adjusted odds ratio, 5.43), lip (3.96), retromolar trigone (3.28) and gingiva (3.13), relative to oral tongue tumours. Exploratory DOI thresholds were 7 mm in chewers (log-rank p = 0.006) and 15 mm in non-chewers (p < 0.001). After adjustment, DOI > 7 mm remained associated with poorer DSS in chewers (hazard ratio, 3.55; 95% confidence interval, 1.32-9.52; p = 0.012), whereas the association for DOI > 15 mm in non-chewers was attenuated (hazard ratio, 1.56; 95% confidence interval, 0.97-2.53; p = 0.069). CONCLUSIONS: Betel-quid exposure was associated with OCSCC at quid-contact subsites. Chewers showed a lower exploratory DOI threshold for DSS than non-chewers.

Authors: Metello Neves LB, Lima BC, Grillo R
Journal: Oral diseases | DOI: 10.1111/odi.70564
Published: 2026-Nov-10

Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Injectable platelet-rich fibrin (i-PRF) is increasingly used for articular temporomandibular disorders (TMD), but it is unclear whether randomised controlled trials (RCTs) report validated diagnostic criteria for participant enrolment. This scoping review maps the diagnostic instruments reported in i-PRF RCTs for articular TMD. It does not assess whether diagnostic systems were applied correctly or the accuracy of diagnoses. METHODS: Following the JBI framework and PRISMA-ScR, RCTs evaluating i-PRF for articular TMD and reporting pain and/or maximum mouth opening were searched in six databases, without date or language restrictions, plus grey literature, trial registries and reference lists. Diagnostic approaches, sample characteristics, imaging, interventions, comparators, follow-up and adverse events were charted. RESULTS: Thirteen RCTs were included. Three reported DC/TMD for enrolment, two from the same research group. Five reported Wilkes staging, three reported imaging without a clinical diagnostic system, and two reported no diagnostic criterion. No trial reported RDC/TMD. CONCLUSION: Fewer than a quarter of i-PRF RCTs reported enrolment using a currently validated diagnostic system. This methodological finding does not indicate whether i-PRF is effective. Future trials should use DC/TMD and report diagnostic procedures in full.

Abstract:
Chidamide is an oral histone deacetylase inhibitor whose use as early maintenance after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) remains insufficiently defined. This prospective single-center Phase 1/2 cohort included all 47 patients enrolled and treated by March 31, 2026. The Phase 2 primary endpoint was 2-year leukemia-free survival (LFS). An exploratory observational comparison used 23 platform-compatible historical comparators, time-dependent maintenance exposure, and propensity-score overlap weighting. Both cohorts received chidamide-containing conditioning. No formal multiplicity adjustment was applied. Treated-cohort 2-year LFS was 78.6% (95% confidence interval [CI], 63.9%-87.9%). In the main weighted model, maintenance exposure was associated with lower hazards of death (hazard ratio [HR], 0.29; 95% CI, 0.09-0.96) and relapse or death (HR, 0.24; 95% CI, 0.09-0.63). LFS associations were more consistent across sensitivity analyses; overall survival was less stable in landmark analyses. Graft-versus-host disease-free/relapse-free survival remained inconclusive. item.title: TTA-MVUM: A Tumor and Text-Aware Multi-View Mamba Framework for Clinical Target Volume Auto-Segmentation in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma Radiotherapy.

item.description:
Authors: Ma X, Wu R, Yi J, Dai J, Men K
Journal: International journal of radiation oncology, biology, physics | DOI: 10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.10.035
Published: 2026-Nov-09
PMID: 43003311



Abstract:
PURPOSE: Accurate segmentation of clinical target volumes (CTV) is critical for the success of radiotherapy in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). Manual contouring is time-consuming and prone to considerable inter-observer variability. Current auto-segmentation models rely exclusively on images, which may lead to sub-optimal accuracy. This study sought to substantially improve CTV auto-segmentation by incorporating tumor and clinical text information with multimodal deep learning. METHODS AND MATERIALS: We retrospectively collected data from 184 NPC patients treated at our institution, with 144 cases allocated for model training and 40 for test. We propose a tumor- and text-aware multi-view UMamba (TTA-MVUM) model with text-image cross-attention modules to fuse visual and textual features. The model input comprised CT images, manually contoured primary gross tumor volume and metastatic lymph nodes, structured text contouring plan extracted by a large language model from electronic health records. Training was guided by a composite loss integrating Dice, cross-entropy and contrastive terms. Model performance was evaluated using Dice, 95% Hausdorff distance and averaged surface distance. RESULTS: The proposed TTA-MVUM model significantly outperformed state-of-the-art image-only and tumor-aware baselines, yielding mean Dice of 0.892 ± 0.035 for high-risk CTV, 0.738 ± 0.149 for low-risk CTV, and 0.889 ± 0.024 for the entire CTV, respectively, with similar improvements for other metrics. Using either tumor information or clinical text alone also surpassed baseline models, but performance remained inferior to the combined approach. CONCLUSIONS: Integrating tumor priors and text guidance can substantially improve the NPC CTV auto-segmentation accuracy and clinical applicability.

Abstract:
PURPOSE: We investigated the risk and prognostic value of pre-treatment nodal progression to inform the safe de-escalation of elective nodal irradiation (ENI) in high-risk oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC). METHODS: We identified patients with p16-negative, clinical T4, node-positive OPSCC treated consecutively with definitive radiotherapy between 2008 and 2021 from a prospectively maintained database. Pre-treatment diagnostic scans were compared against simulation scans to evaluate nodal disease based on pre-specified criteria, growth kinetics, and imaging-detected extranodal extension (iENE). Association of nodal factors and oncologic outcomes were assessed using regression models. RESULTS: A total of 79 patients with a median 30-day interval between diagnostic and simulation scan were identified. Nodal growth was minimal with a median absolute change of + 0.5 cc and growth rate of 0.3%/day. Nodal kinetics and duration between imaging were not prognostic for treatment response. While no patients developed de novo pathological nodal disease, 14% of patients had indeterminant nodes on diagnostic scan, with 27% of these becoming pathological at time of simulation. Total nodal volume was highly correlated with presence of iENE, and was prognostic for locoregional failure (HR = 1.02, p = 0.03), distant failure (HR = 1.02, p = 0.02), and progression-free survival (HR = 1.02, p = 0.05). item.title: A prospective comparative evaluation of dysphagia in surgically resected oral cavity cancers treated by dysphagia optimized volumetric modulated arc therapy (DO-VMAT) versus standard volumetric modulated arc therapy (S-VMAT): DECODE trial.

item.description:
Authors: Mondal P, Nanda SS, Mukherji A, Choubey AK, Dhanush, Dokania S, Patil NH, Krishnan AS, Kumar N, Barman S, et al.

Published: 2026-Nov-09

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Radiotherapy induced dysphagia is a common side effect in post-operative oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC) patients, affecting quality of life (QOL). Dysphagia-optimized radiotherapy reduces dose to dysphagia aspiration-related structures (DARS) while maintaining oncological efficacy. This prospective study compared dysphagia outcomes between DO-VMAT and S-VMAT in resected oral cavity cancers. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This was a two-arm comparative, prospective, interventional study conducted between June 2022 and December 2023 with 50 patients of OCSCC on adjuvant chemoradiation divided in 1:1 ratio to either arm. Acute and chronic toxicities were graded by RTOG criteria. Dysphagia assessment by physician-reported toxicity, 100 ml water swallow test (WST), fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES-DIGEST), and patient-reported QOL using MD Anderson Dysphagia Inventory (MDADI) were performed. Kaplan-Meier method was used to analyze disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS). RESULTS: DO-VMAT achieved significantly lower mean doses to DARS (superior constrictor p = 0.023, middle constrictor p = 0.003, inferior constrictor p = 0.001) compared with S-VMAT. Acute dysphagia rates were comparable (p = 0.238), chronic effects including dysphagia (p = 0.041) and feeding tube dependency (p = 0.041) were significantly lower with DO-VMAT. At 12 months, objective swallowing outcomes favored DO-VMAT, with lower FEES-DIGEST scores (p = 0.018) and higher MDADI composite scores (p = 0.03). 2-year OS (82% vs 78%) and DFS (74% vs 76%) were comparable between S-VMAT and DO-VMAT. CONCLUSION: DO-VMAT is safe and feasible for adjuvant radiotherapy in OCSCC. It significantly reduces late dysphagia and improves patient-reported QOL without affecting disease control or survival.

item.title: Orforglipron for Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Results From 2 Randomized Clinical Trials (ATTAIN-OSA).

Abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common disorder characterized by repeated upper airway collapse during sleep that is associated with reduced quality of life and increased incidence of cardiometabolic disease. OBJECTIVE: To assess the effects of orforglipron on moderate to severe OSA in adults with obesity or overweight, compared with placebo. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Two 52-week, phase 3, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trials were conducted at 66 sites in the US, Argentina, Brazil, China, Czech Republic, Germany, Japan, Mexico, and Taiwan. Adults with moderate to severe OSA and body mass index (BMI; calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 27 or higher were enrolled between November 11, 2024, and July 23, 2025. Final follow-up occurred on July 30, 2026. Trial 1 included patients not receiving positive airway pressure treatment and trial 2 included patients receiving positive airway pressure treatment. INTERVENTION: Patients were randomized (1:1) to receive either once-daily orforglipron (maximum tolerated dose: equivalent to 9-, 14.5-, or 17.2-mg tablet dose) or placebo. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary end point was change in apnea-hypopnea index (AHI, events/h) from baseline to week 52. Seven key multiplicity-controlled secondary end points included change in sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden, the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Short Form Sleep-Related Impairment T-score, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein. RESULTS: A total of 363 patients were randomized in trial 1 (mean age, 48.4 years; BMI, 37.4; AHI, 50.7 events/h; 31.4% female) and 349 patients were randomized in trial 2 (mean age, 51.1 years; BMI, 38.6; AHI, 57.6 events/h; 26.9% female). For the treatment regimen estimand, in trial 1, the mean AHI change was -17.8 for orforglipron compared with -4.5 for placebo (difference, -13.2 [95% CI, -17.7 to -8.7]; P < .001) at 52 weeks. In trial 2, the mean AHI change was -17.3 for orforglipron and -5.3 for placebo (difference, -12.0 [95% CI, -17.1 to -6.9]; P < .001) at 52 weeks. Of 7 key secondary end points, 6 were statistically significant, favoring orforglipron. Gastrointestinal events were the most commonly reported adverse events, occurring in 123 (68.0%) participants randomized to receive orforglipron vs 68 (37.4%) randomized to receive placebo in trial 1 and in 125 (70.6%) participants randomized to receive orforglipron vs 63 (36.6%) randomized to receive placebo in trial 2. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: These results provide evidence for the potential use of oral orforglipron to improve sleep-disordered breathing in adults with moderate to severe OSA and obesity or overweight. Abstract:
PURPOSE: MAPK pathway activation suppresses iodine-handling genes, including sodium-iodide symporter (NIS), contributing to loss of iodine avidity in radioiodine-refractory thyroid cancer. Prior BRAF/ MEK inhibitor re-differentiation trials improved iodine uptake but used empiric 4-6 week treatment. The timing of maximal NIS re-expression remains undefined. We evaluated whether short course dabrafenib plus trametinib restores iodine uptake and provides clinical benefit. PATIENTS AND METHODS: In this multicentre phase II trial, patients with progressive metastatic radioiodine-refractory thyroid carcinoma harbouring BRAFV600E or RAS mutations received dabrafenib and trametinib. I-124 PET/CT dosimetry was performed at baseline and after 2 weeks, with repeat imaging at week 4 post therapy if dosimetry criteria was not met. Radioiodine was administered once criteria was met. The primary endpoint was attainment of predicted lesional absorbed dose ≥20 Gy with I-131 activity ≤300 mCi. Secondary endpoints included RECIST response, progression-free survival (PFS), thyroglobulin response, and safety. RESULTS: Nine of 14 patients (64%) met the dosimetry criteria and received radioiodine; 6 out of 9 (67%) restored iodine uptake within 2 weeks. Among radioiodine-treated patients, best objective response rate within 6 months was 75% by RECIST. Median PFS was 10.8 months. RAS-mutant tumours demonstrated greater lesion regression than BRAFV600E-mutant tumours. Early reduction in stimulated thyroglobulin and preserved FOXE1 nuclear localisation, and higher tumour-to-normal GLIS3 nuclear expression were associated with re-differentiation response. CONCLUSIONS: Short-course dabrafenib/ trametinib can induce rapid re-differentiation within 2 weeks in a subset of patients with MAPK-driven radioiodine-refractory thyroid cancer, supporting individualized BRAF/MEK inhibition duration rather than empiric prolonged treatment.

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: To descriptively compare genomic profiles by human papillomavirus (HPV) status in a Taiwanese multicenter registry with published Western cohorts. METHODS: We reviewed aggregate findings from 290 OPSCC cases in TCOG T1322 (ACTOnco + 440-gene panel) and selected studies from the United States and Europe. Journal: Head & neck | DOI: 10.1002/hed.70541

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dysphagia is a common complication of head and neck cancer (HNC) and its treatment. This study examined swallowing-related quality of life from diagnosis to 12 months after treatment, compared swallowing outcomes across tumor sites and treatment modalities, and identified predictors of moderate-to-severe dysphagia. METHODS: The M. D. Anderson Dysphagia Inventory (MDADI) was completed by 445 patients receiving curatively intended HNC treatment pre-treatment and at 3-, 6-, and 12-months post-treatment. RESULTS: Swallowing-related quality of life worsened during treatment, the poorest scores at 3 months post-treatment; 21.6% reported moderate-to-severe dysphagia, decreasing to 12.5% at 12 months. Risk factors for dysphagia at 12 months included stage IV disease, surgery combined with (chemo)radiotherapy, smoking cessation within 12 months, and pre-treatment sick leave. Patients with cervical carcinoma of unknown primary (CCUP) had the poorest outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: Swallowing function declined during treatment. Patients receiving surgery combined with (chemo)radiotherapy and patients with CCUP are at increased risk of long-term dysphagia and require closer follow-up.

Abstract:
PURPOSE: The present study aimed to evaluate the expression of osteogenic (RUNX2, OPN) and EMT-related (CD44v6, E-cadherin) markers in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), and to investigate their associations with tumor calcification and lymph node metastasis (LNM). METHODS: Surgical specimens from 48 patients with PTC were retrospectively analyzed. Immunohistochemistry was performed to evaluate osteogenic markers (RUNX2 and OPN) and EMT-related markers (CD44v6 and E-cadherin). Protein expression was assessed using semi-quantitative scoring. Subgroup comparisons based on calcification and lymph node status, as well as Spearman's rank correlation analysis, were performed. RESULTS: The proportion of strong positivity (+++) for RUNX2 and OPN was significantly higher in calcified tumors than in non-calcified tumors (RUNX2: 75.0% vs. 45.0%, P = 0.034; OPN: 53.6% vs. 20.0%, P = 0.004). Both markers showed a trend toward a higher proportion of strong positivity in lymph node-positive tumors, although the differences were not statistically significant. Correlation analysis revealed a significant inverse association between OPN and E-cadherin expression (rₛ = -0.377, P = 0.008), suggesting a potential relationship between osteogenic marker expression and EMT-related epithelial phenotype alterations. CONCLUSION: Higher RUNX2 and OPN expression was significantly associated with tumor calcification in PTC, and OPN expression is inversely associated with E-cadherin expression. These findings suggest a potential connection between osteogenic reprogramming and EMT-related phenotypic alterations, indicating that tumor calcification may reflect underlying molecular changes rather than merely a passive dystrophic process.

item.title: Histobiochemical architecture of the vocal folds and the impact of phonotrauma: a state-of-the-art review.
item.dc:creator: Miri M, Lechien JR
item.description:
Authors: Miri M, Lechien JR
Journal: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery | DOI: 10.1007/s00405-026-10781-0
Published: 2026-Nov-08
PMID: 43000556



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To synthesize the current evidence on the histological architecture and biochemical composition of the healthy human vocal fold, and to critically appraise how phonotrauma alters these structural and molecular components. METHODS: Two independent investigators conducted a comprehensive narrative literature search of PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane databases, using MeSH and free-text terms related to vocal fold histology, biochemistry, and phonotrauma. Studies investigating histological, ultrastructural, or molecular modifications of the vocal folds, across human, animal, ex vivo, and cell-line models, were considered eligible. RESULTS: The healthy vocal fold exhibits a multilayered architecture comprising a non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, a basement membrane, and a three-layered lamina propria, with the maculae flavae anchoring the membranous portion at its anterior and posterior insertions. Epithelial barrier integrity is maintained by tight junctions (occludin, ZO-1/2/3, claudins) and adherens junctions (E-cadherin, catenins), while surface hydration is regulated by transepithelial ion transport (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, NKCC1, ENaC, CFTR, TMEM16A) and aquaporin channels (AQP3, AQP4, AQP5). The lamina propria displays a stratified composition of collagen (≈ 43% of total protein), elastin (≈ 9%), hyaluronic acid, sulfated glycosaminoglycans, proteoglycans (decorin, fibromodulin, versican), and glycoproteins (fibronectin), which collectively determine the viscoelastic properties of the cover. Phonotrauma induces epithelial desquamation, microhole formation, downregulation of tight-junction proteins (occludin, ZO-1, E-cadherin), basement membrane thickening, upregulation of inflammatory mediators (IL-1β, TNF-α, COX-2, MMP-8), and progressive remodeling of the extracellular matrix, with species- and time-dependent alterations of fibronectin, decorin, fibromodulin, hyaluronic acid, and collagen subtypes. CONCLUSION: Phonotrauma triggers a coordinated cascade of histological, ultrastructural, cellular, and molecular alterations that disrupt the highly specialized architecture and viscoelastic properties of the vocal fold cover. A comprehensive understanding of these phonotrauma-induced changes is essential to inform preventive strategies, optimize voice therapy approaches, and guide future tissue-engineering and regenerative interventions for voice disorders.

item.title: Evaluation of the HALP score and CALLY index in patients with sudden sensorineural hearing loss.

Authors: Özbuğday Y, Güllüev M, Yücel A, Yücel H, Kaplan D

Published: 2026-Nov-08
PMID: 43000552



Abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate the clinical significance of two immunonutritional biomarkers, the HALP (hemoglobin, albumin, lymphocyte, and platelet) score and the CALLY (C-reactive protein, albumin, and lymphocyte) index, in patients with sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) and to explore their association with hearing recovery. METHODS: This retrospective case-control study included 40 patients with SSNHL and 40 controls with isolated septal deviation. Pre-treatment HALP and CALLY values were calculated from routine blood tests. All patients received oral and intratympanic steroids. Patients were classified as having complete, partial, or no recovery at six months. Exploratory receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were performed, with non-recovery defined as the positive outcome. RESULTS: The HALP score was significantly lower in patients than in controls (median 48.70 vs. 60.96, p = 0.030), mainly reflecting a lower lymphocyte count (p = 0.026), whereas the CALLY index did not differ (p = 0.057). No significant differences in biomarkers, time to treatment, vertigo, tinnitus, or audiogram configuration were found among the recovery groups. In exploratory ROC analyses, CRP (AUC 0.712, 95% CI 0.538-0.885; cut-off ≤ 1.25 mg/L) and the CALLY index (AUC 0.720, 95% CI 0.544-0.896; cut-off ≥ 3.62) discriminated non-recovery, whereas the HALP score did not (AUC 0.547). CONCLUSIONS: The HALP score was lower in patients with SSNHL, but it was not associated with hearing recovery. CRP and the CALLY index showed discrimination of non-recovery only in exploratory analyses with wide confidence intervals. These preliminary, hypothesis-generating findings do not support clinical use and require validation in larger prospective studies.

Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Primary sinonasal extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma (EES) is exceedingly rare, and its clinical characteristics and outcomes remain poorly characterized. We summarized clinicopathological characteristics, treatment patterns, and reported survival outcomes in a structured PubMed-based pooled case series. METHODS: Twenty-four patients, including 3 treated at our institution and 21 identified through a structured PubMed review, were analyzed. Clinical characteristics, tumor extent, treatment, and outcomes were summarized, with exploratory Kaplan-Meier analyses of overall survival. RESULTS: Treatment strategies were heterogeneous and were summarized descriptively without formal comparative treatment-effect analysis. An apparent less favorable survival pattern was observed among patients with documented skull base and/or intracranial involvement, although this finding was sensitive to missing-data assumptions. Three of the four deaths occurred among patients aged 40-59 years, and this age-related pattern was considered descriptive only. Because only four deaths occurred, multivariable prognostic modeling was not performed. CONCLUSION: Primary sinonasal EES predominantly affected younger patients and was more common in women in this cohort. An apparent less favorable survival pattern was observed among patients with documented skull base and/or intracranial involvement, although this finding was sensitive to missing-data assumptions. The age-related pattern was considered descriptive only. Treatment-outcome relationships were summarized descriptively and should not be interpreted as evidence of comparative treatment effectiveness.

item.title: Posterior sinonasal syndrome: pepsin-mediated posterior nasal mucosal injury as a proposed upstream driver of chronic rhinosinusitis. A narrative review of the mechanistic evidence and a testable clinical framework.
item.dc:creator: Gergits FR
item.description:
Authors: Gergits FR
Journal: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery | DOI: 10.1007/s00405-026-10746-3
Published: 2026-Nov-08
PMID: 43000549



Abstract:
PURPOSE: Management of chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) addresses downstream sinus pathology while upstream mucosal drivers receive little attention. This review evaluates the evidence base for Posterior Sinonasal Syndrome (PSS), a hypothesised framework in which reflux-mediated pepsin injury to the posterior nasal mucosa contributes to disease confined largely to the posterior ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses. METHODS: A narrative review of MEDLINE/PubMed and Google Scholar to September 2026 was performed using predefined search terms and eligibility criteria. Each component of the framework was assigned to one of three evidence tiers: established by human clinical data, derived from experimental study, or proposed by the author and untested. RESULTS: Human clinical data establish that pepsin is present in sinonasal secretions of CRS patients above control levels, and that it is recoverable from middle ear fluid in children. Experimental data establish epithelial uptake at neutral pH and pepsin-induced mitochondrial injury with IL-1α and IL-6 release in nasal epithelium. Because mucociliary transport runs anterior to posterior, posterior disease with patent ostiomeatal complexes is not readily explained by anterior spread, the observation from which this framework arose. A candidate radiologic signature is proposed as an objective criterion. It, the endoscopic findings, the aerosolised delivery route and the neurogenic component are untested hypotheses. CONCLUSION: PSS is offered as a testable framework. A diagnostic pathway is proposed for research use in which treatment response functions as a validation outcome rather than a diagnostic criterion. Prospective studies are required before clinical application.

Abstract:
PURPOSE: Salivary gland cancers are rare and heterogeneous malignancies. In recent years, an increasing number of molecular alterations have been identified across the different histological subtypes, leading to the recognition of new entities and refinement of the tumor classification. These molecular alterations are also becoming essential in the diagnostic workup and may carry both prognostic and therapeutic significance. Furthermore, the characterization of these is fundamental for understanding current targeted therapies as well as for the development of new treatments. METHODS: An extensive review of the literature from the last 15 years was conducted, with a specific focus on molecular alterations and targeted therapies in the following salivary gland carcinomas: mucoepidermoid carcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, acinic cell carcinoma, and secretory carcinoma. RESULTS: We provide an updated overview of recurrent and/or specific molecular alterations for each histological subtype and summarize current knowledge regarding their mechanisms of tumorigenesis. Their diagnostic and prognostic implications are also discussed, and existing as well as emerging targeted therapies are reviewed. CONCLUSION: Knowledge of molecular alterations in salivary gland cancers not only enables more precise classification and diagnosis but also contributes to improved prognostic stratification and the development of targeted therapies. It provides the foundation for development of personalized treatment approaches to the most common salivary gland carcinomas.

Published: 2026-Nov-08
PMID: 43000545



Abstract:
PURPOSE: Middle ear cerebrospinal fluid leakage (CSFL) is an uncommon but important cause of adult middle ear effusion, often mistaken for otitis media with effusion. Delayed recognition risks serious infective complications: published series report a median 15.5-month diagnostic delay and meningitis in up to 20% of cases. This paper aimed to develop a practical pathway for recognising, investigating, referring and managing suspected middle ear CSFL in adult ENT practice. METHODS: This pathway combined a retrospective departmental case series, a focused PubMed literature review, and multidisciplinary expert consensus into an evidence-informed, consensus-based pathway for general ENT teams. RESULTS: Seven patients were identified (median age 65 years; four female, three male); middle ear CSFL was recognised after ventilation tube insertion in all cases, and six underwent surgery (transmastoid, middle cranial fossa or subtotal petrosectomy). These cases informed a pathway covering history taking, risk-factor recognition, biochemical confirmation, CT/MRI investigation, senior escalation, meningitis safety netting and skull base MDT referral. CONCLUSION: Middle ear CSFL should be considered in adults with persistent clear otorrhoea after ventilation tube insertion. To our knowledge, this is the first practical pathway developed for general ENT teams and may support earlier recognition and management.

Abstract:
PURPOSE: To map and synthesize the protocols and methodological approaches used in chemical gustometry with taste solutions, focusing on taste assessment methods, the solutions and substances employed, concentration ranges and units of measurement, and the procedures used to determine taste thresholds. METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science. Study selection and data extraction were performed independently and in duplicate by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. The review followed the PRISMA-ScR guidelines and was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework. RESULTS: Of 6,881 records identified, 10 studies met the eligibility criteria, comprising 722 participants across three clinical contexts (oncology/hematology, diabetes mellitus, and otologic disease). The whole-mouth sip-and-spit method and assessment of detection/recognition thresholds were most frequently used. Substantial heterogeneity in methods, tastants, and concentration units limited comparability across studies. CONCLUSION: Standardization of chemical gustometry protocols remains a challenge given the methodological heterogeneity identified, underscoring the need for greater methodological rigor and consistency in future research to improve reproducibility and cross-study comparability.

Abstract:
PURPOSE: This analysis of NRG/RTOG 0424 describes post-treatment changes in neurocognitive function (NCF) and quality of life (QOL) in patients with high-risk low-grade glioma (HR-LGG). METHODS: Patients with HR-LGG were treated with radiation and concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide (RT-TMZ). Standardized NCF tests were performed at baseline, 6, and 12 months. Rates of change in NCF were examined using the reliable change index (RCI) on Hopkins Verbal Learning Test (HVLT), Trail Making Test (TMT), and Controlled Oral Word Association (COWA). Relationships between NCF and subjective cognitive concerns (MOS-CF) were evaluated. QOL was assessed using Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy - Brain (FACT-Br). Longitudinal modeling evaluated predictors of change in NCF and QOL. Cox models assessed the association of baseline NCF with overall survival (OS). RESULTS: From January 2005 to August 2009, 129 evaluable patients were accrued, and 93 completed at least the baseline and one post-treatment NCF/QOL measurement. RCI-determined decline occurred in 50% and 40% at 6 and 12 months, respectively and was most frequent on HVLT (21%, 20%), TMTA (29%, 20%), and TMTB (22%, 14%). MID-determined QOL decline on the FACT-Brain Subscale occurred in about 25% at 6 and 12 months. CONCLUSIONS: Many patients with HR-LGG experience NCF decline in the first year after treatment with temozolomide-based concurrent chemoradiation. QOL remained stable or improved. Ongoing studies with integrated NCF monitoring using these tests will aid clinicians and patients in treatment decisions that seek to consider oncologic and functional outcomes.

Abstract:

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock (AMI-CS) can compromise the administration and absorption of oral P2Y12 inhibitors and carries high ischaemic and mortality risks. This trial assessed whether intravenous cangrelor was non-inferior to crushed oral ticagrelor for short-term clinical outcomes and whether it provided faster and more consistent platelet inhibition in patients with AMI-CS. METHODS: DAPT-SHOCK-AMI was a double-blind trial conducted at 29 hospitals across five European countries (Czech Republic, France, Germany, Poland, and Slovakia). Patients older than 18 years with AMI-CS were randomly assigned (1:1 ratio, stratified by centre, age, sex, presence or absence of ST-segment elevation, and mechanical ventilation) to cangrelor (30 μg/kg bolus followed by an infusion of 4 μg/kg per min for at least 2 h) or crushed ticagrelor (180 mg loading dose). The primary laboratory endpoint was a platelet reactivity index of less than 50% at the end of primary percutaneous coronary intervention. The primary clinical endpoint was death, myocardial infarction, or ischaemic stroke at 30 days. The primary clinical endpoint was analysed for non-inferiority with a prespecified margin of 1 percentage point among all randomly assigned patients who received study treatment. The study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03551964) and EudraCT (2018-002161-19); recruitment and 1-year follow-up are complete, and 5-year follow-up is ongoing. FINDINGS: Between Aug 1, 2018, and Jan 19, 2024, 605 patients (137 [23%] were female) were randomly assigned to cangrelor (n=298) or ticagrelor (n=307); no surviving patients were lost to the 1-year follow-up. The primary laboratory endpoint was analysed in 56 (19%) patients in the cangrelor group and 68 (22%) in the ticagrelor group, and was achieved in 56 (100%) of 56 patients receiving cangrelor and 15 (22%) of 68 receiving ticagrelor (p<0·0001). The 30-day primary clinical endpoint occurred in 112 (38%) of 298 patients receiving cangrelor and 126 (41%) of 307 receiving ticagrelor; non-inferiority was not demonstrated (difference -4 percentage points [90% CI -10 to 3]; Pnon-inferiority=0·13). Major bleeding at 30 days occurred in 19 (6%) of 298 patients receiving cangrelor and 16 (5%) of 307 receiving ticagrelor. INTERPRETATION: To our knowledge, this is the first randomised trial to compare P2Y12 inhibitor strategies specifically in patients with AMI-CS. Cangrelor achieved effective platelet inhibition more frequently than crushed ticagrelor at the end of primary percutaneous coronary intervention. Non-inferiority of cangrelor versus crushed ticagrelor was not demonstrated for the primary 30-day clinical endpoint. These trial findings can inform future trials of P2Y12 inhibition strategies in patients with AMI-CS.
